items.title: Skip the Tools, Make the Outcomes
items.summary: Wroblewski argues that AI lets teams skip building tools entirely and deliver outcomes directly — using a news aggregator that just gives you the news you asked for (instead of a browsable site) as the model.
items.why: A clean framework for rethinking what Cuemath's AI features should be: not tools that help kids practice math, but systems that deliver the understanding they came for.

items.title: Parsing 'Can' from 'Should': How Netflix's Product Team Got Thousands of Creatives to Trust an AI Overhaul
items.summary: Netflix GM of Product Mckenzie Lock explains how they built internal buy-in for AI-assisted dubbing, artwork selection, and content tagging by leading with 'today vs. tomorrow' stakeholder scenarios rather than capability demos.
items.why: The trust-building framework — showing people their workflow today vs. improved tomorrow — maps directly to how Cuemath introduces AI features to tutors, teachers, and parents who didn't ask for it.

items.title: What will make personal AI go big?
items.summary: Julie Zhuo analyzes Meta's Muse consumer AI agent and distills four design principles — approachable, trustworthy, valuable, engaging — that she argues separate consumer AI that reaches mainstream adoption from what stays niche.
items.why: A design-led framework for consumer AI adoption directly applicable to Cuemath: how do you design AI features that parents and kids trust and actually use? Paywalled — worth it for the four-part framework.

items.title: Logos and glyphs grow out of agar and grapevines in Emi Takahashi's graphic explorations of living forms
items.summary: Montreal-based designer Emi Takahashi collaborates with organic materials — slime mould, agar, duckweed — to grow logos, glyphs, and typefaces, translating hidden patterns in natural systems into graphic form.
items.why: A sharp reminder that a design system can be generative without being geometric — the constraint here is biological rather than grid-based. Useful lateral input when thinking about how Cuemath's visual language could have more inherent logic.

items.title: Why designer Merijn Straathof turned a landmark techno album into a playable web-based instrument
items.summary: Dutch designer Merijn Straathof rebuilt Richie Hawtin's DE9 album as an interactive website where all 120 original loops are free to play, chain, and remix — transforming a fixed recording into a participatory instrument.
items.why: A precise case study in turning passive consumption into active engagement: the content doesn't change, but the interface makes the listener a player. That's the core design challenge for Cuemath's math practice — same logic, different domain.
